title: Consequences of a dynamical no-signaling condition for classical-quantum interactions
abstract: Hybrid classical-quantum approaches are instrumental in numerous fields, from condensed matter physics to quantum information science. We recently proposed to describe hybrid systems starting from a set of natural axioms for measurement probabilities without adding any underlying mathematical structure. The so defined probability measures fulfill a no-signaling condition that ensures that instantaneous communication is impossible. We formulate here a dynamical generalization of this condition. It means that, for two independent systems, the outcome probabilities of a measurement made on one of them are not affected by a measurement performed earlier on the other. Analogous requirements are satisfied for usual classical and quantum bipartite systems and violating them would make faster-than-light signaling possible. The dynamical no-signaling condition has important consequences for classical-quantum interactions that depend on the hybrid approach used. For no-signaling hybrid dynamics with classical trajectories, the classical degrees of freedom can influence the quantum ones but the latter cannot react on the former. If pure states of quantum systems remain pure then the dynamical no-signaling condition implies the absence of classical reaction. When all hybrid states are allowed, there are no genuine classical-quantum interactions for no-signaling hybrid dynamics that do not generate correlations between the classical and the quantum degrees of freedom. In all these cases, the proposed condition is equivalent to the convex-linearity of the probability measure transformations describing finite-time evolutions.
summary: This paper rigorously extends the no-signaling principle to describe dynamical interactions between classical and quantum subsystems. It shows that maintaining this causality constraint forces the underlying evolution dynamics to be mathematically equivalent to convex-linear transformations. This has profound implications, restricting genuine non-trivial classical-quantum coupling in time evolution.
main_problem: The paper develops a dynamical generalization of the no-signaling condition specifically for hybrid systems involving classical and quantum degrees of freedom.
main_result: The dynamical no-signaling condition imposes strong constraints on classical-quantum interactions, implying that such interactions must be described by convex-linear transformations equivalent to non-interacting dynamics in certain limits.
method: The analysis involves formulating probability measures for hybrid states and testing the independence of outcome probabilities from ancillary measurements under time evolution operators T. Mathematical tools include information theory (mutual information) and analyzing linear/convex-linear maps.
model_or_system: The system studied is a general hybrid model composed of classical degrees of freedom (defined by a sample space X) coupled to quantum degrees of freedom (described by a Hilbert space H). The dynamics are governed by finite-time evolution operators T acting on the joint probability measure.
key_observables: Outcome probabilities of measurements performed after ancillary pre-measurements; classical-quantum mutual information I(omega); and entanglement measures.
important_parameters: The nature of the hybrid state (pure vs. mixed), the type of evolution T (linear vs. non-linear), and whether all possible hybrid states are allowed.
main_assumptions: The analysis builds upon prior work defining probability measures for hybrid systems and assumes that deviations from no-signaling require non-linear transformations T.
figures_summary: Not specified in the notes, but the structure suggests mathematical derivations proving inequalities related to information loss under evolution.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general framework of hybrid systems and the initial no-signaling condition. It then generalizes this concept dynamically for finite-time evolutions, deriving consequences regarding the directionality (classical influencing quantum but not vice versa) and ultimately proving equivalence to convex-linearity when all states are considered.
why_interesting: This work provides fundamental constraints on how classical information can interact with quantum mechanics in a time-evolution setting, which is crucial for understanding open quantum systems modeling where classical parameters might govern environmental coupling or measurement outcomes.
